findings.title: Foreign Tax Credit shortfall — residual double taxation
findings.detail: Indian tax paid ($23,916) exceeds the US FTC limitation ($13,265) for this year. $10,651 of Indian tax cannot be credited currently and would otherwise be double-taxed.
findings.recommendation: $10,651 is eligible to carry over under §904(c) (back 1 year / forward 10), but WISING is a single-year snapshot — it does NOT persist this carryover across tax years or track it for you. Record $10,651 on Form 1116 Schedule B this year, and re-enter it as prior-year carryover when you run next year's numbers. Also check whether treaty re-sourcing (Art. 25) could reclassify some income to lift the limitation — WISING does not test this automatically.

findings.title: Treaty relief claimed without supporting documents
findings.detail: A treaty position / DTAA rate is being relied upon, but Form 41 is not on file. Indian tax authorities will deny treaty relief u/s 159(8) without a valid TRC, and Form 41 is mandatory u/r 75.
findings.recommendation: Obtain Form 41 before filing. For US residents, request Form 6166 from the IRS (Form 8802 application) well in advance — it can take 6–8 weeks.

findings.title: FBAR threshold breached
findings.detail: Aggregate peak balance across foreign accounts is $25,301, above the USD 10,000 reporting cliff. EVERY foreign account must be reported, not just those over the limit.
findings.recommendation: File FinCEN Form 114 by the due date (auto-extended to Oct 15). Non-willful penalties start at ~$10,000 per violation; willful penalties are far higher.

findings.title: Promoter additional tax on buy-back gains — ₹7,03,248 on top of ordinary capital-gains tax
findings.detail: As a promoter (s.69(2)(b)) on this buy-back, the ordinary 12.5% LTCG tax on the gain is not the end of it: an additional tax brings the combined rate to 30% (non-corporate promoter), and a further 12% surcharge applies on that additional tax specifically — irrespective of total income. Additional tax: ₹6,03,750; surcharge: ₹72,450; cess: ₹27,048.
findings.recommendation: Confirm promoter status (direct/indirect >10% shareholding, or Companies Act/SEBI promoter designation) is correct before relying on this — the additional tax and surcharge do not apply to non-promoter shareholders in the same buy-back at all.

findings.title: Nova Systems Pvt Ltd buy-back: 17 months held — India says STCG, US says LTCG ($1,096 at stake)
findings.detail: This listed buy-back was held 17 months. India requires more than 12 months for LTCG on listed shares, so this is STCG there (taxed at 20%, s.196). The US requires only more than 12 months for LTCG on any asset — no listed/unlisted distinction — so the SAME gain is LTCG under US rules. Recomputed your actual US return both ways: treated as LTCG, US tax is $22,452; treated as STCG (ordinary rates), US tax is $23,549 — a difference of $1,096.
findings.recommendation: Report this gain as LONG-TERM on the US return (Schedule D) even though it's short-term in India — using India's label on the US foreign-capital-gains input would cost roughly $1,096 in overpaid US tax.

findings.title: Advance-tax interest exposure — ss.424/425 (₹74,253)
findings.detail: Advance tax paid (₹0) falls short of the assessed tax (₹14,85,062) this year. At 1%/month simple interest: ₹59,402 under s.424 (shortfall below the 90% floor, 4 months to the non-audit (31 Jul) due date) + ₹14,851 under s.425 (single 15-Mar installment shortfall — presumptive-scheme filers owe 100% in one installment, s.425 proviso). Both keep accruing past the due date until actually paid — this is the exposure AS OF the due date, not a final number.
findings.recommendation: Pay the shortfall before filing to stop s.424 interest accruing further; s.425's quarter-by-quarter amount is fixed once the year ends and doesn't grow. If the year isn't over yet, revise the remaining installment(s) upward.

findings.title: 2 DTAA treaty rate election(s) on file
findings.detail: Layer 1 records a claimed treaty rate on the following India-source income stream(s): dividend @ 25% (Art 10(2)(b)) on ₹5,00,000 [not applied — taxpayer is not NR, see below]; interest @ 15% (Art 11(2)(b)) (no amount entered) [not applied — taxpayer is not NR, see below]. This taxpayer is resident (not NR) under India's own domestic law, so s.207 and every election above has NO effect regardless of income type; residents are taxed on this income at slab rates instead. If the taxpayer is genuinely meant to be NR, check the residency determination; if not, these elections are moot. Layer 1 does NOT show Form 41 on file — every one of these elections is at risk of being denied and defaulting back to slab/domestic rates without it.
findings.recommendation: Obtain Form 41 before relying on any of these elected rates — without it, the payer/assessing officer can withhold or assess at the full domestic rate shown above instead.

findings.title: India residency status may not match the facts on file — derived RNOR, recorded ROR
findings.detail: Re-deriving India's residential-status determination from the same raw facts Layer 1's own wizard uses (day-count, the 4-year lookback, RNOR sub-status conditions, employment/PIO-visit exceptions, s.6(1A) deemed-residency, incorporation/POEM, or control-and-management, depending on entity type) produces RNOR, but the recorded final_india_residency_status is ROR.
findings.recommendation: Re-run the Layer 1 India residency wizard, or verify the underlying residency facts were entered consistently — this looks like a wizard or data-entry error.

findings.title: Controlled Foreign Corporation — Form 5471 required (GILTI/Subpart F not yet quantified)
findings.detail: Layer 1 records the US person owning ≥10% of a foreign corporation (Indian company on file), so Form 5471 applies and GILTI / Subpart F can accelerate US tax on undistributed Indian profits before any dividend is paid. WISING flags the exposure from the ownership data but does NOT yet compute a GILTI/Subpart F inclusion amount — that requires the entity's tested income, E&P and qualified business asset investment (QBAI), which Layer 1 doesn't collect today.
findings.recommendation: File Form 5471 regardless. To quantify GILTI/Subpart F (and evaluate the §962 election against India's MAT/credit), collect the Indian company's tested income, E&P and QBAI — until then, treat this as a required-filing flag, not a computed liability.

findings.title: Related-party cross-border transactions — transfer pricing documentation may apply
findings.detail: Layer 1 records a related-party cross-border ownership link (US person owning ≥10% of a foreign/Indian corporation). Any transactions between you and that related entity this year — service fees, cost allocations, loans, guarantees, IP licensing — must be priced at arm's length under India's s.92-92F and the US's parallel §482 regime. WISING does NOT evaluate whether pricing is arm's-length; it only flags that the relationship exists.
findings.recommendation: If related-party cross-border transactions occurred this year, confirm Form 3CEB certification and Rule 10D documentation requirements (India side) and §482 documentation (US side) with a transfer-pricing specialist — penalties for missing documentation run 2% of transaction value, up to 200% for concealment.

findings.title: Trump Account (§530A) contribution cap exceeded
findings.detail: Contributions of $11,000 across 2 child(ren) exceed the $5,000/child/year cap (combined across all contributors — parents, family, employer all draw from the same limit). A $1,000 one-time federal seed contribution applies to the 1 child(ren) born 2025-2028 — separate from, and not counted against, the $5,000/year cap.
findings.recommendation: Excess contributions are not automatically rejected by the custodian in every case — verify the aggregate against all contributors and consider a corrective withdrawal before the account's growth compounds on an over-contribution.

findings.title: 6 income head(s) taxed under both codes — see reconciliation
findings.detail: The same income is taxed in India (its own Act) and the US (the IRC): Interest, Capital gains, US Salary / Wages, US Interest, US Dividend, US Capital gains. Overlapping exposure of $234,304 is what the FTC / §159 relief resolves. Some heads are planning-grade estimates pending line-item inputs.
findings.recommendation: Open the Cross-Basis Reconciliation on the Filings tab to see each head on both bases, then relieve the overlap via Form 1116 (US) / Form 44 (India).

findings.title: Dual residency resolved under DTAA Article 4 → US
findings.detail: Both India and the US met residency, and the Layer 1 Article 4 tie-breaker resolves treaty residence to US for the overlapping period. WISING has applied this to the tax and FTC computation below; the loser jurisdiction is taxed on a source basis.
findings.recommendation: Keep Form 8833 (US) and TRC + Form 41 (India) on file to support the position.

findings.title: Brought-forward losses fully set off this year
findings.detail: All eligible prior-year losses were absorbed against this year's income: ₹2,50,000 STCG loss vs. slab-rate STCG (s.69 unlisted buy-back). The India tax computed above already reflects this — no residual carry-forward remains.
findings.recommendation: Confirm the set-off is reported correctly on Schedule CFL/BFLA of the ITR, matching the ordering above.

findings.title: Form 44 — required for the Indian FTC claim
findings.detail: Foreign income / foreign tax is present, so India requires Form 44 (with Schedule FSI and TR) on or before the ITR due date to allow FTC u/s 90/91.
findings.recommendation: WISING flags Form 44 (with Schedule FSI/TR) as required on the filing checklist, using the FSI/TR figures already computed above — actually preparing and e-filing it on the income-tax portal ahead of the ITR due date is still a manual step.

findings.title: Tax-year apportionment: Indian FY ↔ US CY (computed)
findings.detail: India taxes Apr–Mar; the US taxes Jan–Dec. WISING splits the Indian FY across US calendar years — $67,315 into CY2026 and $22,438 into CY2027 (even-earning assumption (Apr–Dec vs Jan–Mar)) — and apportions the US calendar year into the Indian FY (9/12 + 3/12).
findings.recommendation: See the FY ↔ CY Apportionment panel on the Filings tab for the period-matched figures behind Form 44 (India) and Form 1116 (US). Planning-grade — refine with per-transaction dates at filing.

findings.title: FX conversion basis is an approximation
findings.detail: Cross-border amounts are normalized at a flat 83 INR/USD. Statutory FTC computations require the telegraphic-transfer buying rate on the relevant date (Rule 115 / SBI TTBR).
findings.recommendation: Re-price each foreign income and tax item at the correct per-transaction rate before filing; the flat rate is for planning visibility only.

documents.why: AMT preference items (commonly an ISO exercise, or the SALT-cap add-back) push tentative minimum tax above the regular tax for the year.

scopeNotes.title: GAAR is not evaluated
scopeNotes.body: India's General Anti-Avoidance Rule can recharacterize arrangements that lack commercial substance — a facts-and-circumstances judgment no rules engine can safely make. WISING flags mechanical conflicts only; whether an arrangement invites GAAR scrutiny remains a professional call.

scopeNotes.title: STT is not computed as a levy
scopeNotes.body: Securities Transaction Tax charged on trades (raised on F&O by Finance Act 2026) isn't calculated here. The stt_paid flag on each transaction drives the capital-gains regime (s.196/198 vs s.197) — the levy amount itself is neither a tax credit nor a capital-gains deduction, so nothing downstream depends on it.

scopeNotes.title: Your obligations as a TDS deductor aren't tracked
scopeNotes.body: The Withholding page covers tax withheld FROM this taxpayer's income. Duties in the opposite direction — deducting TDS on payments the business makes to vendors, contractors, or professionals — aren't monitored as a compliance obligation in their own right, though the resulting s.40(a) expense disallowance for TDS failures (and s.40A(3) cash-payment / s.43B(h) MSME-overdue disallowances) does flow into business income (Phase 1).

scopeNotes.title: Clubbing amounts are taken as entered
scopeNotes.body: Spousal and minor-child clubbed income entered in Layer 1 is taxed as given. WISING doesn't trace asset transfers between family members to detect clubbing that should have been reported but wasn't.

scopeNotes.title: FICA/FUTA levies aren't computed
scopeNotes.body: Employee and employer Social Security/Medicare/unemployment payroll taxes are a separate tax base from income tax. Only the pieces that touch the 1040 are computed: Additional Medicare 0.9%, self-employment tax, and the W-2 withholding shown on the Withholding page.

scopeNotes.title: FATCA Chapter 4 withholding is institution-side
scopeNotes.body: The 30% FATCA withholding regime (IRC §§1471-1474) applies to payments to non-compliant foreign financial institutions — banks' problem, not yours directly. Where it touches an individual is the US-person self-certification banks request, which is tracked with your documents.

scopeNotes.title: Document-upload extraction is simulated
scopeNotes.body: Every "upload to auto-fill" feature in Layer 1 (Form 26AS, Lower-TDS certificate, bank statements, property documents) is a demo simulation with representative values — not live OCR. Figures sourced from an upload should be treated as manually-entered until real extraction ships.

scopeNotes.title: MLI does not affect the India-US treaty
scopeNotes.body: The US never signed the OECD Multilateral Instrument, so the India-US DTAA text is untouched by it — unlike India's treaties with the UK, Netherlands, or Singapore. Verified; nothing to apply.

scopeNotes.title: Treaty text current as modeled
scopeNotes.body: The India-US DTAA has not been amended since the 2000 protocol. Every treaty rate and tie-breaker rule in this engine reflects the treaty as it stands.

trace.detail: For Individuals and HUFs with Business or Professional Income maintaining books, or receiving remuneration/interest as a partner in a firm. Mandatory if disqualified from ITR-4. Reasons: Total income exceeds ₹50,00,000 (₹70,74,471); Capital gains beyond the s.198-only allowance (STCG and/or non-s.198 LTCG present); Brought-forward losses on file. Layer 1 India hasn't produced its own recommendation for this profile (itr_recommendation.form is unset) — this is WISING's own independent computation, run unconditionally, not a hedge pending the frontend.
trace.citation: CBDT notified the AY 2026-27 ITR forms 2026-03-30 (corrigendum 2026-04-10). Eligibility rules verified against that notification 2026-07-12 — re-check each filing season, since CBDT re-notifies forms (and sometimes changes eligibility) annually.
